label: R1:repair
name: Shaft-bottom XRT sorting, hoist-bound mines
mech: Anchor: domestic X-ray transmission (XRT) sorters at the shaft bottom reject waste lumps before hoisting, and the rejects go straight into stope backfill. The repair moves it from "freeing concentrator capacity" to deep mines where the 2.1 km shafts set the limit, such as Skalisty and the Talnakh/Oktyabrskoye deep levels. There every tonne of waste rejected below ground is replaced by ore in the fixed skip capacity. With the fines (about 35% of ore) bypassing the sorter, metal hoisted per year rises ×1.095 at Selebi-type results (15% rejected, 2% metal lost) and ×1.36 at stringer-type results (44%, 4%). After counting the metal lost for good in the backfill, metal NPV is still ×1.085–1.31 over a 30-year reserve at 14%. Two or three 150 t/h units cover 2 Mt/yr hoisted. Rejects of at most 0.41 t per t of ore fit in the backfill needed (0.44–0.67 t per t), so no tailings go to the surface. The design is restricted to cuprous/stringer and massive ores at contacts. Disseminated Norilsk-1 and Maslovskoye ore is left out (16% metal loss at 23% rejection on disseminated test ore), as are mines where hoisting is not the limit.
value: Each extra tonne of Ni-eq from a hoist-bound deep mine costs $5.0–8.3k by sorting against $6.7–12.6k from a new deep shaft, 1.2–1.8× cheaper. It comes in about 2–3 years instead of about 10 years of shaft sinking.

label: OLD:repair
name: Pre-staged flood-crest barges
mech: Anchor: a loaded barge waits out the ice drift in a sheltered backwater and leaves on the flood crest. Repair: load it in autumn while it is still afloat at a deep berth, so nothing is loaded through ice. It winters in a backwater at least 2.5 m deep, and it is used on a tributary that is navigable only on the spring flood, where there is just one trip a year anyway. With a modelled 12-day recession, a convoy arriving 5–10 days late loses 35–62% of its load. A barge pre-staged at the river mouth goes in full.
value: About 3,100 rub/t against 4,700–11,300 rub/t on that leg today (1.5–3.6x). On the Kolyma main stem the gain is only about 14%.

label: P1:repair
name: Diesel-sized first line, nuclear expansion
mech: Anchor: a diesel-sized starter on leased domestic or unrestricted gensets comes first. The nuclear-sized expansion follows when the floating units deliver, and the gensets then move to other sites. Repaired design: the starter is no longer a separate 6 Mt/y plant. That version still fails: $8.3k/t Cu net against $2.0k/t for the full plan, and a $45m a year margin on $1.08bn of capex. Instead, line 1 of the Baimskaya plant now under construction (start planned for end-2028) runs at a throughput sized to 80 MW of leased gensets. It uses the SAG mill and one of two ball mills at a coarser grind, on the highest-grade benches. That gives 15 Mt/y of ore at about 0.51% Cu (the first-decade head implied by the feasibility study), 67 kt Cu and 98 koz Au a year. It burns 117 kt of diesel a year at $0.30/kWh, which takes 6 tanker calls into Pevek and needs 174k m³ of tankage. With fuel coming in and concentrate going out on the same trucks, that is about 7,000 loads a year: 20 a day on the all-season road, or 78 a day on a winter road alone. Net cash cost is $1.95k/t Cu after gold credit. Line 1 is also commissioned on diesel, so the ramp-up is done before the reactors arrive.
value: Each year the floating units slip, the bridge earns about $0.52bn of cash margin ($0.29bn at Cu $8k / Au $2.8k) from a plant whose $8bn would otherwise cost about $1.2bn a year to carry idle. Waiting idle earns nothing in those years.

label: P2:repair
name: Size Sever to hulls
mech: The anchor is unchanged: each month Bukhta Sever receives only what the Russian-built Arc hulls can lift, about 1.54 Mt/y per 69 kt hull on the 15.5-day Murmansk cycle (1.2 Mt/y if winter stretches the cycle to 20 days). The allocation is reversed. Vankor-cluster oil (about 11.6–12.3 Mt in 2026–27) stays on the existing Vankor–Purpe line. That line is rated 25 Mt/y and has 12.7–13.4 Mt/y spare. The oil goes to the export outlet it already sells to, not to domestic refineries, which are already crude-long. South is the cheaper margin: about $57/t to an Asian buyer via Transneft and Kozmino, against about $86/t north via Sever, Murmansk and Suez. The north carries only Payakha oil, and Payakha drilling is scheduled to Zvezda Arc hull deliveries, so no well is drilled whose oil cannot be lifted. Because of that, no surplus ever has to go south and the Payakha–Vankor segment never needs reverse flow.
value: Delivered cost per tonne falls by about $29/t on every Vankor tonne kept south, and holding back 15–25 Mt/y of Payakha capacity by 2–3 years saves $2.4–5.8bn in present value. That is about $80–190 per tonne of the capacity deferred, against the published plan of 30 Mt/y in H2 2027, which needs about 19 hulls that do not exist.

label: P3:repair
name: Availability as capacity
mech: Anchor: one parts registry pools spares across the Western-built underground fleet, ranks failure modes by Ni-eq tonnes lost, and sends the worst part families to domestic reverse-engineering and casting first. The stock is re-optimised every quarter from measured mean time between failures (MTBF). With 6 mines and a 9-month grey-import lead time, a pooled stock is 46–62% the size of separate site stocks for the same service. With the same budget, the chance a part is on hand when needed rises from 80% to 99.5% (Poisson model). Ranking by Ni-eq sends the first effort to the rich-ore fleets: one lost LHD-hour there costs about 6.3 t Ni-eq, against 1.2 t on Norilsk-1 ore (5.2×). That makes the programme 1.7× more effective than ranking by machine-hours. Base case: availability rises about 7 percentage points, output by about 29 kt Ni-eq/yr (3.6% of the group), at about $2,700 per added tonne. Gains count only while the mines, not the concentrators, are the limit (taken as 60%). It breaks even if domestic parts last at least 0.30× as long as the original parts.
value: Each added tonne costs about $2,700, roughly 0.35× the $7,300–8,100 of a brownfield capacity stage. Group full cost falls about 2.6% within 6–18 months, which is real but not a 1.5× cut.

label: synthesis
name: Gated diesel bridge plus pooled spares
mech: (1) Norilsk, starting now: build one spares registry for the Western-built underground fleet. Spares are pooled across 6 mines and ranked by Ni-eq lost per machine-hour (6.3 t on rich ore, 1.2 t on Norilsk-1). Domestic reverse-engineering and casting start with the worst part families. The programme winds down as the BelAZ/MoAZ JV fleet (Sosnovoborsk, about 150 machines/yr) replaces those machines. The corrected effect is +8 to +29 kt Ni-eq/yr (central +15 kt) at about $5.4k per added tonne. (2) Baimskaya, decided at a gate in Q4 2027: if the first two RITM-200S floating units are not at mooring trials by then, they cannot power line 1 when it is ready in Q1 2029 (RAEX, Apr 2026). In that case Baimskaya leases about 80 MW of domestic gensets (Kolomna or UDMZ 1.5–2.5 MW units) and runs line 1 at about 65 MW average. That gives 12.2 Mt/y of ore (not 15), 48 kt Cu and 77 koz Au a year. It burns 146 kt/y of diesel at 0.225 kg/kWh, which costs about $0.31/kWh. Diesel comes from Far East refineries through the Bering Strait in 7–8 tanker calls into Pevek. That route keeps clear of the Kara Sea icebreakers Part 2 needs. The fuel is held in about 173k m³ of tankage (about $173m), built on cooled piles to bedrock with full secondary containment, which is the Ambarnaya lesson. Concentrate (222 kt wet a year, 5–6 ships of 40 kt) is stockpiled at Nagleynyn for the 3–4 month shipping season. The gensets leave when the floating units arrive. (3) Oil and gas: no change. Both Part 2 ideas only reproduce current practice: Vankor oil goes south on Vankor–Purpe, Payakha oil goes north as far as the hulls allow, and Yamal LNG uses Kildin ship-to-ship transfer plus summer cargoes east.
value: Copper: expected value is +$185m (+$66m at $8k Cu / $2.8k Au), and the bridge breaks even if the floating units slip 0.44 years. Life-of-mine full cost is 0.98× the no-bridge case for a 1-year slip and 0.955× for a 2-year slip. First metal comes 1.05 years earlier on expectation, with a 35% chance of no gain. Nickel-equivalent: group full cost goes from about $10.05k to $9.97k/t Ni-eq (−0.85%, range −0.1% to −2.5%) within 6–18 months, and the gain fades over 3–5 years. LNG and oil: 1.00× current practice.

label: synthesis
name: Half bridge on the winter road
mech: Same Q4 2027 gate, but at 40 MW average: 7.5 Mt/y of ore, 30 kt Cu, 48 koz Au, 90 kt/y of diesel and about 106k m³ of tankage (about $106m). That needs about 6,600 road loads a year, or about 51 a day on a 130-day winter road. That is about a third of the record daily rate on Canada's Tibbitt–Contwoyto winter road (about 158 a day). So it does not depend on the 800 km Baimskaya–Nagleynyn all-season road, of which only 250 km was built at last report. Line 1 is commissioned and run in on diesel. Norilsk and oil and gas are handled as in IDEA 1.
value: Expected value is +$102m (+$29m at low prices), with break-even at 0.50 years of slip. Net cash cost is $2.0k/t Cu at base prices and $3.0k/t at low prices. The life-of-mine cost gain is about half of IDEA 1's, but this version still works if the road slips along with the floating units.
